statement: In adults treated in emergency departments for cannabis hyperemesis syndrome, dopamine-blocking medicines given by injection (haloperidol, droperidol) were associated with faster relief and shorter stays in both studies described in a 2024 systematic review (Sabbineni et al., 2024; AMSTAR 2 critically low; 106 patients). In one small randomized trial (30 patients; Ruberto et al., 2021, as described in the review), haloperidol reduced pain and nausea more than ondansetron, a standard anti-sickness medicine, after 2 hours (difference 2.3 cm on a 10 cm scale), with more treatment success (54% against 29%), less need for rescue medicines (31% against 59%) and earlier discharge (3.1 against 5.6 hours); in one chart review of 76 patients, those given droperidol had shorter hospital stays (6.7 against 13.9 hours). Both medicines caused acute dystonia (sudden muscle spasms) in a few people: two return visits after haloperidol and one case after droperidol; two people were drowsy after droperidol. The evidence is small and at high risk of bias. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: Some hospital medicines that block dopamine, a brain chemical, are used for cannabis hyperemesis syndrome. In one small fair test, haloperidol eased pain and sickness more than a usual anti-sickness medicine and people went home sooner. In another study, people given droperidol left hospital sooner. Both medicines gave a few people sudden muscle spasms. The studies were small, so we cannot be sure.
population: Adults treated for cannabis hyperemesis syndrome in emergency departments
exposure: Intravenous haloperidol or droperidol given in hospital (doses are study conditions in the study card)
comparator: Intravenous ondansetron (randomized trial); patients not given droperidol (chart review)
outcome: Pain and nausea scores, treatment success, rescue medicines, time to discharge, length of stay, adverse events
magnitude: Haloperidol against ondansetron: mean difference 2.3 cm in combined pain and nausea at 2 h (p = 0.01); success 54% against 29%; rescue antiemetics 31% against 59%; any medicine 31% against 76%; discharge 3.1 (SD 1.7) against 5.6 (SD 4.5) h (p = 0.03). Droperidol: hospital stay 6.7 against 13.9 h (p = 0.014); discharge after last antiemetic 137 against 185 min (p = 0.002). Acute dystonia: 2 return visits after haloperidol, 1 after droperidol.

evidence.locator: Table 3, Ruberto et al. row (p. 500); Results, Studies on dopamine antagonists (p. 501, left column)
evidence.extracted: Randomized trial (Ruberto et al.; ondansetron n = 17, haloperidol n = 13 with two doses pooled): greater reduction in abdominal pain and nausea at 2 h with haloperidol (mean difference 2.3, p = 0.01); treatment success 54% against 29%; rescue antiemetics 31% against 59%; benzodiazepines 8% against 41%; any medicine 31% against 76%; time to discharge 3.1 (SD 1.7) against 5.6 (SD 4.5) h, p = 0.03; two return visits for acute dystonia after haloperidol, none after ondansetron.

evidence.locator: Table 2, Lee et al. row (pp. 496-497); Results, Studies on dopamine antagonists (p. 501, left column)
evidence.extracted: Chart review (Lee et al., 37 given intravenous droperidol, 39 not): total hospital stay 6.7 against 13.9 h (p = 0.014); time to discharge after the last antiemetic 137 against 185 min (p = 0.002); two patients drowsy, one acute dystonia that responded to benztropine, no cardiac adverse events; 30 of 689 records excluded for missing data.

evidence.locator: Results, paragraph after Table 2 (p. 498); Discussion, 2nd and 4th paragraphs (p. 501); Limitations (p. 502)
evidence.extracted: Both randomized trials were at high risk of bias (loss to follow-up); the authors call the evidence for dopamine antagonists limited in number and quality and preliminary, list dystonia, arrhythmias and drowsiness as their side effects, and note the haloperidol trial compared against ondansetron in a small convenience sample.

risk_of_bias.note: The trial is at high risk of bias (loss to follow-up, convenience sample); the droperidol evidence is a retrospective chart review; both seen through a critically low review.

inconsistency.note: Both studies favour the dopamine antagonist.

indirectness.note: Two different medicines, each studied once; worded for the two.

imprecision.note: 30 and 76 patients; no confidence intervals for the main differences.

grade.reasoning: Starting from the randomized trial (high), risk of bias -2 and imprecision -1 give very low. Status replicated at the level of the medicine class: two independent studies, of two different medicines and designs, point the same way; each medicine has been studied once. The randomized trial is inside the review, so the trial and the review must not be cited as independent support.
